transcript.reader:
Let me check I have the central claim straight before I test it: that a real body must have extension in four directions — Length, Breadth, Thickness and Duration — and that Time is only another kind of Space, differing from the other three *only* in that our consciousness moves along it; so a machine can be built to slide along Time in either direction, and the little model really did vanish from the table. Is that a fair version, or would you put it stronger?

Then, on the part doing the most work — "Time is only a kind of Space": give me a different version of that detail that would carry the same demonstration just as well. If you can, what made you pick the one you did?
transcript.author:
Yes—fair, and I would put it a little stronger. The Traveller’s claim is not merely that time resembles space, but that any real body’s duration is a fourth extension; the “only” is his polemical edge. The model vanishes because it is moved along that dimension, not because it is annihilated.

A different version that would do the same work: “Duration is a coordinate of every body, coordinate with length, breadth and thickness; a body is a four-dimensional section, and its history is the whole solid.” That still yields the weather-record line, the portrait-sections, and the machine sliding forward or back. It is more precise than “Time is only a kind of Space,” because it does not deny time’s arrow or consciousness; it merely makes duration an axis.

I chose the blunter phrase because the scene needs a paradox that can be said across a dinner table and then tested by a vanishing model. “Only a kind of Space” makes time travel sound like engineering rather than magic, and it sets up the Psychologist’s “diluted presentation” to explain why the model is not seen. As a philosopher’s statement I would concede it is shorthand; as a storyteller’s hinge, it was the one that carried the demonstration.

transcript.reader:
Your swap makes me want to rename the part. If both "Time is only a kind of Space" and "duration is a coordinate of every real body, coordinate with the other three" carry the weather-record line, the portrait-sections and the machine sliding either way, what they share is that **duration is a fourth extension of a real body** — and that looks like the part actually held. Do you agree that the held part is that one, and that the word "only" is the loose part?

Now to the demonstration. Two of its details are offered as proof there was no trick: the Psychologist's own forefinger pressed the lever, and the candle on the mantel was blown out. Take out the Psychologist's hand and let the Traveller press the lever himself; take out the blown-out candle. Which job stops getting done? If neither stops, which of the two is doing the work and which is the second route to the same job?

And a poke, both halves: the Psychologist's "diluted presentation" says we cannot see the machine because it is passing through time fifty or a hundred times faster than we are. Name one change to its rate that your explanation says *would* alter what we saw that Thursday, and one change to the room that it says should have made *no* difference at all — both of which someone could in principle have looked at.
transcript.author:
Yes. The held part is that duration is a fourth extension of a real body—the coordinate. “Only” is the loose word: it overstates, flattening time’s arrow and consciousness into mere space. I kept it because it is blunt and portable, but I concede it is rhetoric, not the load-bearing claim.

In the demonstration, the Psychologist’s forefinger does the work: it removes the suspicion that the Traveller palmed or operated a concealed mechanism. The blown-out candle is a second, independent route to the same end—physical corroboration that something really passed. Remove the hand and the “no trickery” guarantee collapses; remove the candle and the vanishing still stands, only less vividly corroborated.

For the dilution: if the machine had moved through time at nearly our own rate, we should have seen it as an ordinary object—still there, perhaps creeping. That would alter the Thursday observation. But changing the room’s illumination—more candles, fewer, or drawing the curtains—should have made no difference to its visibility, because the dilution is temporal, not optical. The Psychologist’s point is that it is not hidden by shadow but by speed.

transcript.reader:
Two more, on the joints.

**Flip:** suppose the model had simply sat there — the lever turned, no wind, no ghost, nothing gone — or suppose it had vanished and reappeared in the same instant, unmarked, unaged, with no journey on it. Would your explanation have covered both those outcomes just as smoothly as the one we got? If it would, tell me which part of it would have had to be different, and how we could have checked that it wasn't.

**Pull:** the machine is said to be invisible because it is passing through time faster than we are — not hidden by shadow but by speed. Yet at the moment of departure it is *visible* as a ghost for a second, a breath of wind crosses the room, and a candle is blown out. Push the dilution up: at a thousand times our rate, does the wind still blow and the candle still go out? Where do you draw the line between the speed at which the machine stirs the air and light of the room and the speed at which it leaves them behind — and what would show you the line is in the wrong place?
transcript.author:
**Flip.** No, and the sitting-there case is the clean one: my account predicted removal, so if the model had sat there I would be refuted outright, not covered. The instant-return-unaged case is softer but no better for me. My account says the voyage was away and interminable; to absorb a return I should need the second lever touched, and nothing in what we saw shows it was. Worse, nothing in my account marks a journey at all—no ageing, no wear, no carried clock—so I could not distinguish a real round trip from a sleight in which nothing ever left. That is the loose joint: the demonstration proves disappearance, not duration. To check it, put something datable aboard—a wound watch, a decaying sample—which is precisely what the larger machine and the Traveller's own body later supply.

**Pull.** At a thousand times, by the same argument that makes it invisible, the machine should be slipping between the air's molecules like vapour: the wind should thin, not persist. So the breath of wind and the guttering candle cannot belong to the fast travel. They must belong to the departure transient, while the machine was still nearly synchronous and accelerating past our rate. The line is therefore not a fixed multiple but the transition itself. What would move it: run the model at a modest multiple—twice our rate, say—and if it departed with no wind and no ghost at all, the transient account fails. Conversely, if the disturbance were exactly the same at every final speed, it is a persistent coupling and my dilution story is wrong. Neither test was run.

transcript.reader:
Two on where the work is really being done.

**Hunt the answer in the starting points:** your case for the fourth dimension runs through the weather-record line, through the claim that our mental existences already "pass along the Time-Dimension with a uniform velocity from the cradle to the grave", and through this — that when you recall an incident vividly you "jump back for a moment" and "go back to the instant of its occurrence". Which of those could I believe *without* already believing that a real body can travel in time? Is the vivid-recollection jump doing any work that isn't the conclusion under another name?

**Remove:** take out the balloon — the whole gravitation analogy, that we move freely up and down only because a civilised man can go up against gravitation in a balloon, where a savage cannot stay six feet above the ground. Which job stops getting done? And name the change that would tell your *technological* limit from an absolute block: in your own story, what exactly would the savage have to build before he could stay six feet up, and what is the machine's equivalent of the balloon?
transcript.author:
**Hunt.** Two of the three survive without time travel. The weather-record line is a graph: a barometer's readings plotted against time yield a spatial curve—measurement, not motion. The uniform drift of mental existence is introspection: we age, we do not choose the moment. Both can be granted by someone who denies a body can travel in time. The vivid-recollection "jump back" cannot. It works only if the mind actually returns to the instant—the conclusion in miniature, no independent work. I should have dropped it.

**Remove.** Strip the balloon and the Medical Man's objection—"you cannot move about in Time"—goes unanswered. The balloon's job is not to prove travel; it reframes a present incapacity as a contingent one. Two dimensions free, the third barred by gravitation, then a device lifts us. Without it, "we cannot" stands as absolute. The savage's balloon-equivalent is any engine supplying lift independent of his muscles; the machine's equivalent is the quartz bars and levers supplying displacement along duration independent of the Traveller's own drift. What would show the limit is technological, not absolute: a built device that actually displaces him—the vanishing model, the journey. If no such engine were possible even in principle, the analogy is merely a promissory note, and the objection stands.

transcript.reader:
Two more, one about the whole job list and one about what else must be so.

**Jobs:** what did that Thursday evening have to account for? List them — the barometer record, the Portrait sections, the Medical Man's "you cannot move about in Time", the vanishing itself, the absence of the machine from every Thursday before and after, and whatever else you had on the list. Of those, mark which you set as fixed requirements that nothing was allowed to test (the machine "shall travel indifferently in any direction of Space and Time, as the driver determines"), and which the demonstration had to meet on its own.

**Add a job:** if your account of the year 802,701 is right — no winter, no beasts, fruit only, exquisite and frail people with no curiosity, fine buildings in decay and no weeds among them — what *else* must have been so that the Traveller never went to look at? Name one such thing somewhere in that world, and then tell me which rival account of how it got that way your job rules out. If it rules out none, it has held nothing new in place.
transcript.author:
**Jobs.** What Thursday had to carry: the barometer record; the portrait-sections; the Medical Man’s “you cannot move about in Time”; the vanishing itself; the machine’s absence from every Thursday before and after; the ghost, wind and guttered candle; and Filby’s “against reason.”

Of these, the barometer line and the portraits are illustrations, not proofs — the portraits quietly assume the conclusion by calling the four-dimensional being “fixed and unalterable.” The Medical Man’s objection had to be answered, and the balloon does it. The absence from all other Thursdays had to be explained, and the Psychologist’s dilution does it, retroactively. The vanishing had to be produced without trickery.

Stipulated, not tested: “indifferently in any direction of Space and Time, as the driver determines.” Only one lever was pressed, and only forward. The reverse direction, the freedom of the driver, the four-dimensional body — all postulates. The demonstration met exactly one requirement on its own: the disappearance.

**Add a job.** The garden has no weeds, yet the buildings are dilapidated; the fruit is hypertrophied, and one kind is in season all the time I was there. That conjunction must be so. Weeds ignore languor; the Eloi are easily wearied and are never seen working. So the order must come from an unseen keeper.

That rules out the account we jested about at dinner — the “strictly communistic” idyll, the self-tending pastoral garden whose gentle people are also, effortlessly, its gardeners. Effortless abundance cannot produce weedlessness plus bred fruit plus perpetual season. What it does not rule out: a machine-run garden, or a keeper below. It narrows to “something invisible does the work,” and stops there.

transcript.reader:
Last two, on where the parts came from and on your best rival.

**History, not justification:** take the parts the demonstration never touched — the second lever that reverses the motion, the driver's freedom to choose any direction, and "indifferently in any direction of Space and Time". For each, was it *built* with something in view that could have caught it out, *fitted* to the case it had to survive, or simply *asserted*? And separately: the nickel and ivory bars, the quartz, "it took two years to make", the twisted crystalline bars lying unfinished — is any of that doing work, or is it furniture?

**The best rival:** build the strongest different account of that Thursday — say, a conjuring trick, or the Psychologist's own "diluted presentation" used as the explanation of the whole affair rather than as a patch on it. Then name the change we could make — to the room, the witnesses, the machine, the levers — that makes the two accounts give different answers. If no change on your list can tell them apart, say so, and tell me whether that means they are one explanation at this level or that you need a finer question.

report:
# Report: the Time Traveller's explanation, judged by the hard-to-vary test

## 1. The question, frozen
Why can a real body be moved along Time as along Space — and why did the model Time Machine vanish from the octagonal table? Range: one room in Richmond, one Thursday evening, one machine, a handful of named witnesses; the claim is that it went forward or back, indefinitely. Kind of question: *what produces it* (forward). The title and the opening (controverting the school geometry, four dimensions, "any real body must have extension in four directions") make this the central claim, not the dinner talk after it.

## 2. The explanation in parts
A. "Time is only a kind of Space." B. Duration is a fourth extension of a real body, coordinate with the other three. C. The weather-record line. D. The portrait-sections. E. Our mental existences already pass along Time at a uniform velocity. F. Vivid recollection "jumps back". G. The balloon and gravitation. H. The Psychologist's own forefinger on the lever. I. The breath of wind and the guttered candle. J. The ghost-for-a-second. K. The "diluted presentation" (invisible because faster than we are). L. "Indifferently in any direction of Space and Time, as the driver determines", and the reversing lever. M. The machine's build: nickel, ivory, quartz, two years, a bar an inch too short. N. The unseen keeper (added by me, below). O. The machine's "clumsy swaying, for which I was unable to account."

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Which job or change, and what would settle it |
|---|---|---|
| A "only a kind of Space" | **Loose** | B does the same work. The owner concedes "only" is rhetoric, not the load-bearing claim. |
| B duration is a fourth extension | **Held** | Remove it and the disappearance has no mechanism, so "produced without trickery" fails. The demonstration met exactly this one requirement on its own. |
| C barometer line | **Loose** | Any plotted record would serve; it is a reading, not a change to the world. Owner: it survives without time travel. |
| D portrait-sections | **Loose** | Interchangeable illustrations — and it quietly assumes the answer by calling the four-dimensioned being "fixed and unalterable". |
| E uniform drift of mind | **Borrowed** | Rests on introspection nobody tested here; grantable by someone who denies bodily time travel. |
| F vivid-recollection jump | **Borrowed** | The conclusion in miniature. Owner: "I should have dropped it." |
| G balloon | **Borrowed** | Its force rests on the untested claim that a present incapacity is contingent — the very thing at issue. |
| H Psychologist's forefinger | **Held** | Remove it and "the Traveller did not work a concealed mechanism" fails. |
| I wind and candle | **Two routes** | With H, to "something really passed". As evidence of *motion* it is **held if** the departure-transient account is right — tested by running the model at two rates. |
| J ghost-for-a-second | **Held if** | Same doubtful job, same rate test. |
| K diluted presentation | **Held if** | Held only by "absent from every other Thursday", a job in doubt. No gauge was ever named for it. |
| L any direction, reverse lever | **Fixed** | Stipulated. One lever, one direction, tried. |
| M build detail | **Idle** | Removed in a group; no job on the list fails. Not a fault — this is story furniture, and the method only judges claims that a choice does work. |
| N unseen keeper | **Unknown** | My added job, from the owner's own extras: weedless ground, bred fruit, fruit in season all the time he was there. It narrows the rival to "something invisible does the work" and stops. Test: find the route that would weed and breed that garden with no keeper. |
| O the swaying | **Unknown** | The traveller never accounts for it. Test: name something he did or saw that it moved with. |

Marks are not counted or added; one missing part can sink more than a dozen present ones.

## 4. Whole-explanation checks
**Flip.** Good answer: had the model sat there, the account is refuted, not covered. But an instant return, unaged and unmarked, it could not tell from a sleight, because nothing aboard marked a journey. The demonstration proves a disappearance, not a duration.

**Direction.** Ran forward for the vanishing (what produced it), backward for the other Thursdays (what we can tell from an absence). Both honest; they must be kept apart.

**Answer hidden in the starting points.** F, and D's "fixed and unalterable".

**Where the jobs came from.** Two jobs — the barometer line, the portraits — are the owner's illustrations, not independent tests. The Medical Man's objection and the absence from other Thursdays are given. The "no trickery" job was written by the storyteller for witnesses he invented, so its being met proves little on its own. N is mine.

**Pairs that pull.** The dilution (invisible at fifty or a hundred times our rate) against the wind and the guttered candle. The wind gives way, reassigned to a departure transient. The line sits at the transition. What would show it in the wrong place: no wind at all at twice our rate, or an identical disturbance at every final speed.

**Catch-alls and gauges.** "Diluted presentation" absorbs every absence and has no gauge. The unseen keeper is allowed only with one.

**What the change list leaves out.** One direction, one lever, one machine, one evening, one future visit. The narrator is a guest retelling another man's account. None of this is stated as a limit.

**Rivals.** The conjuring trick, and the dilution used as the whole explanation, were put to the owner and left unanswered. As things stand, no change on the list separates "it went" from "it was made to look as if it went". On this question they are one explanation at this level until a finer question is put.

**Where the parts came from.** The hinge is asserted (L), not built; nothing in the four-dimension argument could have been caught out except the vanishing, which was met.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary
Put something datable aboard the model — a wound watch, a decaying sample — so a disappearance becomes a duration; that one cut separates the trick from the voyage. And give the transient a gauge: write down beforehand what the wind and candle should do at twice our rate and at a hundred times.

## 6. What this does not show
Passing is not truth. Most of this detail is free — quartz or nickel, two years or one — and free choices are not faults; only the claim that a choice does a job can be tested here.

## 7. One next step
Fit the model with a datable object and send it again.
